blocks.text: Simonis, in his Lexicon and in the Arcanum Formarum p. 660, thinks the word עכבר is compounded from the verb עכר, which he supposes has the same meaning as the Arabic عرك [ʿarak] he rubbed, and from the word בר, so that it denotes the animal rubbing grain. How frigid this is, anyone will feel at once. Nor do I like any better what Michaelis put forward in Supplemm. ad Lexx. vol. 5, p. 1908, referring the Hebrew עכבר to the Arabic عُكَبٌ [ʿukabun] nimble, brisk.

The singular جُرَذٌ [juradhun] is explained in the lexicons as: a species of field mouse. Under the name جِرْذ [jirdh], Dschird, Shaw described this animal in Travels p. 156 of the German trans., from which it is clear that it is the mus Glis with a hairy tail, the body dark ash-grey above, whitish below, or the sciurus canus subtus albidus of Linnaeus, p. 155, ed. 13, the μυωξον [myōxon] of Oppian, Cyneg. 2, 574.

Bochart passed over the Syriac translator, who put ܥܘܟܒܪܐ, a word that signifies both a mouse and a creeping disease, one that twists itself like a serpent, on the testimony of the lexicographer Bar Bahlul. To this belongs the view of Hensler too, chief physician to the king [II, 431] of Denmark, that by the word עכברים in 1 Sam. VI, 5. not mice are meant but carbuncles, perhaps venereal buboes. Michaelis reports this conjecture, from a letter Hensler sent him, in the Supplemm. vol. 5, p. 1909, and not without approval: “There is,” he says, “something in the whole narrative that urges us to understand buboes or piles of this kind. Among the evils that had afflicted the Philistines, 1 Sam. V makes no mention of mice, which so troubled the translators that the LXX and the Vulgate translator added mice at 1 Sam. V, 6.; Houbigant approved this, but no manuscript has confirmed it. We are freed from all doubt if the mice of Chapter VI are much the same as עפלים, carbuncles, or a kind of tumour or ulcer.” But he soon adds: “Yet verse five of chapter VI seems to stand in the way and to favour mice that lay waste the field: עכבריכם המשחיתים את הארץ.”

“It is certain that female mice gnaw metals and other hard bodies which they cannot eat, namely at the time when they are pregnant. Nor do only mice act so then, but also the females of the other animals that belong to the family of the Glires. — It may be that the teeth of pregnant females are severely affected, and the animals ease this pain by gnawing or biting.” So Beckmann on Aristotle, On Marvellous Things Heard ch. 24, p. 57.
Examples of fields laid waste by mice in the West Indies, from travel accounts, will be given by Oedmann, Vermischte Sammlungen fasc. 2, ch. 3, p. 45.

Oedmann, loc. cit., thinks that both glires [rats] (Ratzen) and sorices [shrews] are comprised under the Hebrew name עכבר, led chiefly by the fact that some of those who have visited Eretz Yisrael report that the fields there are laid waste by both these kinds of animals. This argument would hardly satisfy others. I would think the Hebrew names שפן and עכבר differ thus: the former signifies the Syrian sorex, Arab. وَبْر [wabr] (cf. note 3 to the preceding Chapter), the other, עכבר, the mus jaculus, on the authority of the Arabic dialect, in which عَكْبَر [ʿakbar] and يربوع [yarbūʿ] are nearly synonyms; see Bochart above and p. 1015.
